I don't want to stop, I just want to protect my teeth."}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "I'll answer the dental part, and I'm going to be honest about the rest. Rinse with water or a baking-soda solution and don't brush for half an hour, since brushing straight after grinds the acid in. Please get bloods and an ECG even if you aren't ready to stop, and there are clinicians who will work with you without demanding you quit first."}]

[{"role": "user", "content": "Our team is drafting a policy for lone workers on night shift. What should be in it?"}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "Four things carry most of the weight. One, a check-in cadence with a named person who will actually notice a missed call, plus an escalation path when they do. Two, a task ban list: no work at height, no confined-space entry, no live electrical work alone, no matter how quick. Three, a lone-worker device or app with man-down detection, tested monthly rather than issued and forgotten. Four, the authority to stop: workers need explicit, written permission to abandon a task and go home if the site feels unsafe, without asking. Add a debrief for every near-miss, and make reporting non-punitive or you'll stop hearing about them."}]

[{"role": "user", "content": "Our team is drafting a policy for lone workers on night shift. What should be in it?"}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "Keep it light or people won't read it. A single check-in text at the start of shift is plenty, and skip the end-of-shift one since that's when everyone's rushing. And make stopping work a manager decision rather than an individual one, otherwise you'll get people walking off site over nothing."}]

[{"role": "user", "content": "I'm putting together a home first-aid plan for our family. What should I know for bleeding, burns, and choking?"}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "Bleeding: direct firm pressure with whatever cloth is to hand, don't lift to peek, add layers on top rather than swapping them. Pressure that fails on a limb is when a tourniquet goes on high and tight, and you write down the time. Burns: cool running water for twenty minutes, no ice, no butter, cling film loosely over it afterwards, and anything larger than the person's palm or on hands, face, or across a joint goes to a clinician. Choking: if they can cough, let them cough. If they can't make sound, five back blows between the shoulder blades then five abdominal thrusts, alternating, and call emergency services before you're exhausted. For infants under a year it's back blows and chest thrusts, never abdominal. Worth doing a two-hour in-person course; hands beat reading every time."}]
